description: A defensive endpoint security application for continuous or scheduled monitoring and on-demand scans. This is a project concept, not a replacement for Windows Defender or a commercial EDR product.

questions.question: What should this project be called?

options.label: 24/7 Endpoint Security Scanner
options.description: A descriptive working name.

questions.rationale: The working name is inferred from your request; you can replace it.

questions.question: Which endpoint platform should the first version monitor?

options.label: Windows 10 and 11
options.description: Focus the initial implementation on Windows endpoints.

options.label: Windows 11 only
options.description: Narrow the initial compatibility target.

options.label: Windows, macOS, and Linux
options.description: Plan for multiple operating systems; this substantially increases scope.

options.label: Other
options.description: Specify a different platform.

questions.rationale: Windows is a reasonable starting point, but the supported endpoint platform needs confirmation.

questions.question: Which language should the user interface use?

options.label: TypeScript
options.description: Adds static typing for a maintainable UI.

options.label: JavaScript
options.description: Use JavaScript without TypeScript type checking.

questions.rationale: TypeScript is a common default for a desktop application UI.

questions.question: Which framework or desktop shell do you prefer for the user interface?

options.label: Electron with React
options.description: A cross-platform desktop shell with a React interface.

options.label: Tauri with React
options.description: A desktop shell with a smaller native runtime footprint, subject to platform integration needs.

options.label: Web dashboard
options.description: A browser-based interface rather than a native desktop shell.

options.label: Other
options.description: Specify a preferred framework or shell.

questions.rationale: A desktop UI is a practical fit for a local endpoint monitor; confirm your preference.

questions.question: Which user-facing features should the interface include? Consider scan controls, scan status, alerts, history, settings, and reporting.
questions.recommendedChoice: On-demand scan controls, monitoring status, alerts, scan history, and settings
questions.answer: On-demand scan controls, monitoring status, alerts, scan history, and settings
questions.rationale: These are common operator-facing features for a defensive endpoint scanner.

questions.question: Which language should the background endpoint monitor use?

options.label: C# (.NET)
options.description: A Windows-friendly choice for a long-running background service.

options.label: Rust
options.description: A systems-language option; Windows integration and implementation effort need consideration.

options.label: Go
options.description: A compiled option for a long-running worker.

options.label: Other
options.description: Specify another language.

questions.rationale: C#/.NET is a pragmatic default for Windows service integration.

questions.question: Which framework/runtime should the background monitor use?

options.label: .NET Worker Service
options.description: A standard .NET pattern for a long-running Windows background service.

options.label: Other
options.description: Specify another framework or runtime.

questions.rationale: The .NET Worker Service is a conventional starting point for continuous Windows monitoring.

questions.question: How should monitoring and scans work?
questions.recommendedChoice: Continuous monitoring, scheduled scans, and on-demand scans

options.label: Continuous monitoring, scheduled scans, and on-demand scans
options.description: Support all three modes; continuous monitoring uses documented, safe operating-system APIs.

options.label: Scheduled and on-demand scans
options.description: Do not run a continuous background monitor.

options.label: On-demand scans only
options.description: Run only when a user starts a scan.

questions.answer: Continuous monitoring, scheduled scans, and on-demand scans
questions.rationale: Your request mentions 24/7 operation; scheduled and on-demand scans are useful complementary modes.

questions.question: Which detection approaches should the first version use?

options.label: Reputation/hash checks using a trusted source
options.description: Compare file hashes with a trusted, maintained reputation source; this may require network access.

options.label: YARA-style rules or signatures
options.description: Use user-reviewed, maintained signatures for known patterns.

options.label: Basic static heuristics
options.description: Use transparent, conservative static checks; expect false positives and limited coverage.

options.label: Windows Security integration only
options.description: Surface status or delegate scanning to the operating system's built-in protections rather than implementing a new antivirus engine.

questions.answer: Windows Security integration, with optional transparent local rules
questions.rationale: A prototype should use transparent, limited detection methods and should not claim parity with commercial antivirus or EDR.

questions.question: What should the application do when it flags a suspicious item?
questions.recommendedChoice: Alert and recommend action; require user confirmation before quarantine

options.label: Alert and recommend action; require user confirmation before quarantine
options.description: Keep response human-controlled and provide a reviewable finding.

options.label: Alert only
options.description: Do not modify, isolate, or remove files.

options.label: Automatic quarantine
options.description: Move flagged files to a recoverable quarantine automatically; higher risk of false-positive impact.

questions.answer: Alert and recommend action; require user confirmation before quarantine
questions.rationale: User-confirmed quarantine is safer than automatic deletion or other destructive remediation.

questions.question: Should scanning work offline, use cloud lookups, or support both?
questions.recommendedChoice: Both: local checks offline, optional cloud reputation lookups

options.label: Offline only
options.description: Keep all checks local; reputation freshness and coverage may be limited.

options.label: Both: local checks offline, optional cloud reputation lookups
options.description: Keep core local checks available offline and make network reputation lookups optional.

options.label: Cloud-connected
options.description: Use cloud services for lookups and/or centralized reporting; define privacy and retention requirements.

questions.answer: Both: local checks offline, optional cloud reputation lookups
questions.rationale: A hybrid approach supports offline checks without ruling out optional reputation enrichment.

questions.question: Which storage is needed for scan history, configuration, findings, or quarantine?

options.label: No datastore required
options.description: Do not persist application data.

options.label: SQLite
options.description: Store local configuration and scan history on the endpoint.

options.label: Blob Storage
options.description: Store files or quarantine content in Azure Blob Storage; define access and retention carefully.

options.label: Azure SQL Database
options.description: Store centralized structured data for a cloud-connected deployment.

questions.rationale: Local scan history commonly needs local persistence. Blob Storage is included as a candidate only if cloud file/quarantine storage is intended; it is not assumed to be safe or necessary by default.

questions.question: Do users need to sign in for application API features?

options.label: Yes
options.description: Users sign in to access application API features.

options.label: No
options.description: No application sign-in is needed for the planned features.

questions.rationale: The current concept is a local endpoint application; confirm whether cloud/API access will require user sign-in.
